title: Part 3.I — The Dialectic of Constitutions
role: The volume's longest chapter (79 pp.) and its master applied-dramatism case study. Burke deploys the full pentad and substance vocabulary on the analysis of constitutional language — primarily the US Constitution but ranging across anarchist, anarcho-syndicalist, and laissez-faire constitutional projects. The opening half develops the methodological apparatus ('Necessity for Representative Case', 'The Two Circles', 'Terminal as Anecdote', 'Representativeness of Total War'), reasserts that constitutions are 'addressed by Agents to Agents', and introduces the constitution-behind-the-constitution distinction (the implicit scene-of-scenes that any explicit constitutional document presupposes). The second half works case studies (anarchism, anarcho-syndicalism, laissez-faire, Coleridge's pantisocracy, judicial review via Marshall, the role of the president, political rhetoric as secular prayer) and closes with the dialectics of federation. The chapter doubles as a methodological template for the dissertation's empirical-adaptation chapter: every Phase 3 deliverable inherits this chapter's demonstration that the pentad can be operationalized at document-corpus scale.
